etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English dissh, disch, from Old English disċ (“plate; bowl; dish”), from Proto-West Germanic *disk (“table; dish”), from Latin discus. Doublet of dais, desk, disc, discus, disk, and diskos.

definitions.definition: A vessel such as a plate for holding or serving food, often flat with a depressed region in the middle.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Judges v:25:
quote.text: She brought forth butter in a lordly dish.

definitions.definition: The contents of such a vessel.
(metonymically) A specific type of prepared food.

quote.citation: 1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Iulius Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: Let's carve him a dish fit for the gods

definitions.definition: (in the plural) Tableware (including cutlery, etc, as well as crockery) that is to be or is being washed after being used to prepare, serve and eat a meal.
(telecommunications) A type of antenna with a similar shape to a plate or bowl.

quote.citation: 1993, Westwood Studios, Lands of Lore: The Throne of Chaos, Virgin Games:
quote.text: Have you seen the new apothecary? I think her name is Sadie. What a dish!

definitions.definition: (dated) The state of being concave, like a dish, or the degree of such concavity.[1]
A hollow place, as in a field.[1]

quote.text: As I topped the ridge I missed my first shot at a sharptail that flushed from a grassy dish.

He and Stratemeier raced across the flats and dropped into the canyon, climbed swiftly through it and came out at the topside trail , which went straight south through the timber until it dropped into a small grassy dish surrounded by rock peaks.

quote.citation: 2006 September 14, Richard Holmes, Martin Marix Evans, A Guide to Battles: Decisive Conflicts in History, OUP Oxford, →ISBN:
quote.text: Daylight revealed that the so-called summit was near the edge of a shallow, stony dish, which terminated abruptly in steep slopes, and actually offered poor fields of fire.

quote.citation: 2008, Paul Byrd, Free Byrd: The Power of a Liberated Life, page 4:
quote.text: He said, "I don't like your chances at the dish [home plate] tonight."

quote.citation: 2009, Loren Long, Phil Bildner, Magic in the Outfield, page 40:
quote.text: At the plate, Graham pounded the dish three times, just like Bubbles did whenever he was up,  […]

quote.citation: 2014, Conor Kelley, The Catcher's Handbook, page 87:
quote.text: Also, if you end up getting to the baseball, your pitcher needs to be covering home plate, which pitchers occasionally forget to do. However, if the ball stays near the dish and you have a pitcher on the mound who isn't a space-case, you've got a good shot to get the runner out.

definitions.definition: (mining, archaic) A trough in which ore is measured.[1]
(mining, archaic) That portion of the produce of a mine which is paid to the land owner or proprietor.[1]

quote.citation: 1989 December 24, Abe Rybeck, “Liberation Without Permission, Pleasure Without Apology”, in Gay Community News, volume 17, number 24, page 5:
quote.text: We've been a very lucky community: We've had GCN to collect our deep dish and write it up as political discourse. GCN is not just another clipboard of polite press releases. GCN is the sticky questions, the sweet moments, and the dirty stories that make up our lives.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To put in a dish or dishes; serve, usually food.
(informal, slang) To gossip; to relay information about the personal situation of another.
(transitive) To make concave, or depress in the middle, like a dish.[1]
(slang, archaic, transitive) To frustrate; to beat; to outwit or defeat.
